PROPOSED RESOLUTION

CELEBRATING THE 100TH BIRTHDAY OF JOSEPH LEVAR JR.

WHEREAS, Joseph J. Levar Jr., a lifetime resident of the Jefferson Park community will celebrate the remarkable milestone of his 100th birthday on November 22, 2026; and

WHEREAS, he has witnessed a century of extraordinary history and change while building a lasting legacy rooted in family, faith and devotion to his community; and

WHEREAS, Joseph J. Levar Jr. was born into the Our Lady of Victory Parish on November 23, 1926, to Joseph and Myrtle Levar.  Joseph was one of three children, brother Robert Levar and sister Marilyn Gast, all who attended Our Lady of Victory School.  Joseph went on to graduate from Carl Schurz High School where he was a member of the ROTC where he qualified for pre-flight.  When he graduated from high school, he immediately enlisted in the Army.  He attended Northwestern University, where he graduated with a degree in business and marketing; and 

WHEREAS, Joseph married the love of his life, Dolores Berney Levar on May 13, 1950, at Our Lady of Victory Church and went on to have six sons, all of whom graduated from Our Lady of Victory school, St. Patrick High School and various colleges; and  

WHEREAS, Joseph worked for Coca-Cola USA for 40 years.  He began as a travelling salesman and worked his way up to Prestige Account Executive before retiring in 1986; and

WHEREAS, Joseph was an active member of his Northwest Side community participating in the Men’s Choral Club and President of the OLV Holy Name Society as well as a Eucharistic Minister at Our Lady of Victory Parish, a proud member of the Kiwanis Club of Portage Park which he formed in 1990, a precinct captain for the 45th Ward Democratic Organization for 45 years, and Institutional Rep for Boy Scouts Portage District; and

WHEREAS, Joseph and Dolores were married for over 65 years before Dolores’ passing on February 16, 2016.  Joseph, an avid lifelong Cubs fan, proposed to Dolores, also an avid lifelong Cubs fan, in the Wrigley Field bleachers and they attended hundreds of games together.  Joseph believes that Dolores was acting as an angel for the Cubs after her passing and that is what helped them win the World Series that same year; and 

WHEREAS, Joseph is the loving father of the Honorable Patrick J. Sr. (Mary Ann), Michael (Joan), Thomas (Debra), Gerald (Robbin), Joseph III, and Daniel (Robin).  He has 13 grandchildren and 15 great grandchildren who he absolutely adores and talks about with pride to anyone that will listen; and

WHEREAS, Joseph J. Levar Jr. was a devoted husband and brother and is a devoted father, grandfather, great-grandfather, brother-in-law, uncle, cousin, and cherished friend to many, and richly deserves the warm and fond wishes of his family and friends as he marks this birthday milestone; and

WHEREAS, on behalf of the entire 12th District, Cook County Commissioner Bridget Degnen extends her personal tribute to Joseph J. Levar Jr. on this momentous occasion in recognition of his remarkable life and his many years as a valued resident of the 12th District of Cook County; and

NOW, THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED, that we, the Cook County Board of Commissioners, assembled this 14th day of October 2026, do hereby congratulate Joseph J. Levar Jr. on his 100th birthday and extend our best wishes for continued happiness, good health, and many more cherished moments with his family and friends; and

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that a suitable copy of this resolution be presented to Joseph J. Levar Jr. as a symbol of our admiration, appreciation, and warmest wishes on this extraordinary milestone.

il-17031-bos-matter-81458.title:
PROPOSED RESOLUTION

REQUESTING THE COOK COUNTY BOARD’S CRIMINAL JUSTICE COMMITTEE TO CONVENE A HEARING REGARDING THE RESPECTIVE AUTHORITY, RESPONSIBILITIES, AND INVESTIGATIVE OVERSIGHT PROCEDURES OF THE COOK COUNTY SHERIFF’S OFFICE AND THE OFFICE OF THE INDEPENDENT INSPECTOR GENERAL

WHEREAS, the Cook County Board of Commissioners recognizes the importance of transparency, accountability, fairness, and public confidence in the administration of County government and its public safety institutions; and

WHEREAS, the Cook County Sheriff’s Office is an independently elected office responsible for carrying out significant law enforcement, correctional, and public safety responsibilities under Illinois law; and

WHEREAS, the Cook County Office of the Independent Inspector General (OIIG) is established under County ordinance to promote integrity, accountability, and responsible government through the exercise of its legally authorized oversight and investigative functions; and

WHEREAS, both the Sheriff’s Office and the OIIG perform important public functions, and clarity regarding their respective legal authority, responsibilities, and procedures is essential to effective government operations; and

WHEREAS, questions have arisen concerning the scope of the OIIG’s authority to review certain investigations involving Sheriff’s Office personnel and the respective responsibilities of both offices in addressing allegations of misconduct; and

WHEREAS, the OIIG has identified and communicated recommendations concerning investigative procedures, including:

The identification, documentation, and appropriate consideration of allegations arising from complaints, video recordings, reports, and other available evidence;

The establishment and consistent application of procedures for informational complaints and external referrals, including appropriate management notification, documentation, and disposition;

The application of consistent investigative standards, including witness interviews, examination of relevant evidence, identification of potential subjects, and documentation of investigative findings and decisions; and

WHEREAS, differences in interpretation or implementation of these recommendations warrant further examination to better understand the legal, operational, and administrative considerations of the respective offices; and

WHEREAS, concerns have also been raised regarding the handling and disposition of certain complaints involving Sheriff’s Office personnel, including a reported incident involving allegations that an employee reported for duty while impaired and possessed an allegedly unlawful firearm; and

WHEREAS, the inclusion of such allegations in this Resolution is solely for the purpose of identifying matters appropriate for procedural review and shall not be construed as a determination that misconduct occurred or that any investigation was improperly conducted; and

WHEREAS, the OIIG has established a Public Safety Oversight Unit to address matters within its asserted oversight responsibilities, and questions concerning the unit’s legal authority, operational scope, coordination, and relationship with existing investigative functions warrant examination; and

WHEREAS, the OIIG has requested that the Cook County Board’s Criminal Justice Committee convene a public hearing to examine these matters; and

WHEREAS, the Cook County Board’s Criminal Justice Committee has an interest in ensuring that County public safety institutions operate within their respective legal authority and maintain appropriate standards of transparency, accountability, due process, and public trust; and

WHEREAS, a hearing would provide an appropriate forum for the Sheriff’s Office, the OIIG, and other relevant parties to present their respective positions, explain existing procedures, and identify opportunities for improved coordination and clarity; and

WHEREAS, the purpose of such a hearing is to gather information, clarify applicable legal and administrative responsibilities, and evaluate existing policies and procedures without prejudging the conduct, legal position, or conclusions of any individual or office.

NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the Cook County Board of Commissioners requests that the Criminal Justice Committee convene a hearing for the following purposes:

1.	Legal Authority and Jurisdiction: Examine the respective legal authority, jurisdiction, and responsibilities of the Cook County Sheriff’s Office and the OIIG under applicable Illinois law and Cook County ordinances.

2.	Investigative Standards and Procedures: Review the policies, procedures, and standards used to receive, investigate, document, refer, and resolve complaints involving Sheriff’s Office personnel.

3.	 Recommendations and Responses: Examine the OIIG’s investigative recommendations and the Sheriff’s Office’s responses, including any legal, operational, or administrative considerations influencing their implementation.

4.	Complaint Review and Disposition: Review the procedures followed in selected matters involving allegations of employee misconduct, including the reported impaired-and-armed employee incident, to determine whether existing policies provide appropriate standards of documentation, review, accountability, and due process.

5.	Public Safety Oversight Unit: Examine the purpose, legal authority, responsibilities, and operational scope of the OIIG’s Public Safety Oversight Unit, including its relationship with existing Sheriff’s Office investigative and accountability functions.

6.	Interagency Coordination: Identify opportunities to strengthen communication, coordination, and the appropriate exchange of information between the Sheriff’s Office and the OIIG while respecting their respective legal responsibilities.

7.	Potential Improvements: Consider whether additional policy guidance, administrative procedures, interagency agreements, or legislative clarification may be appropriate to strengthen transparency, accountability, and public confidence.

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the Criminal Justice Committee shall conduct the hearing in an impartial manner, affording the Sheriff’s Office, the OIIG, and other invited participants a fair and reasonable opportunity to present information, respond to questions, and explain their respective positions; and

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the Committee shall invite testimony from the Cook County Sheriff, the Independent Inspector General, appropriate representatives of their respective offices, relevant legal and administrative experts, and other individuals whose participation may assist the Committee in fulfilling its oversight responsibilities; and

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the Committee shall conduct its proceedings in accordance with applicable law, including requirements concerning confidentiality, personnel privacy, due process, and the protection of ongoing investigations; and

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that nothing in this Resolution shall be interpreted as a finding of misconduct, an endorsement or rejection of any disputed legal position, or an attempt to interfere with the lawful duties and independent authority of either office; and

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that following the hearing, the Committee may consider appropriate recommendations concerning legislative clarification, administrative coordination, or improvements to investigative oversight procedures based upon the information presented; and

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the Clerk of the Board shall transmit a copy of this Resolution to the Chair of the Criminal Justice Committee, the Cook County Sheriff, and the Cook County Independent Inspector General.

MARY ELLEN GUEST, IN MEMORIAM                    

WHEREAS Almighty God in His infinite wisdom has called Mary Ellen Guest from our midst, and

WHEREAS Mary Ellen Guest was the loving mother of James Schulte (Katie Grogan) and Johnny Schulte, proud grandmother of Jack and Mairead Schulte, devoted daughter of the late Ronald and Helen (nee Keane) Guest, loving and dear sister of Cathy Guest (Tom Gerk), Eileen Guest, Ret. Sgt. CPD, Tim Guest (Ruth Degnan), and Patrick Guest (Laura Arvesen Guest), and beloved aunt to many nieces and nephews, and

WHREAS Mary Ellen Guest was deeply rooted in Chicago’s South Side, dedicating her career and being committed to its residents and neighborhoods.  She began her career in Democratic political campaigns and later served as executive director of Working in the Schools (WITS) and A+ Illinois, and

WHEREAS Mary Ellen Guest joined the Chicago Bungalow Association on March 1, 2010, and led the organization for more than 16 years.  Under her leadership, CBA advanced its mission of helping residents preserve their homes and remain in their communities through energy-efficiency programs, homeowner education, neighborhood advocacy, and housing preservation, 

WHEREAS from 2018 through 2025, CBA and its partners completed more than 9,400 energy-efficiency projects, providing no-cost improvements to income-qualified households throughout Chicago and the surrounding region. These figures represent only part of the energy-efficiency assistance delivered during Mary Ellens tenure, and  

WHEREAS Mary Ellen believed that effective community service began with listening to residents.  She personally participated in dozens of neighborhood and community events each year and helped build relationships that connected homeowners with resources for repairs energy efficiency, property taxes, estate planning, and other needs, and

WHEREAS Under Mary Ellen’s leadership, CBA’s sustained advocacy helped make health and safety funding available within utility programs, allowing homeowners with repairs needed to receive improvements that had previously been out of reach, and 

WHEREAS during Mary Ellen’s tenure, CBA expanded its energy-efficiency work beyond single-family homes to include two-and three-flat buildings and other Chicago-style vintage housing, and

WHEREAS Mary Ellen supported the CBA’s growth as a trusted source of free homeowner education, with 17 webinars reaching more than 5,000 attendees and participation in more than 70 community events in 2024, and

WHEREAS Mary Ellen supported CBA’s partnership with artist Tonika Lewis Johnson on UnBlocked Englewood, combining home repairs with resident-led neighborhood improvements while addressing the lasting effects of discriminatory housing practices, and 

WHEREAS Mary Ellen was a passionate follower of news and politics, she believed public service should create tangible improvements in people’s everyday lives, and 

WHEREAS all who knew her will attest that Mary Ellen Guest was a kind and compassionate woman, virtuous of character and gentle in spirit, admired and respected by her many friends and neighbors, and dearly loved by her family, now therefore

BE IT RESOLVED by the Board of Commissioners of Cook County that the Board does hereby extend its deepest condolences and most heartfelt sympathy to the family and many friends of Mary Ellen Guest and joins them in sorrow at this time of loss, and

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that this text be spread upon the official proceedings of this Honorable Body, and an official copy of same be presented to the family of Mary Ellen Guest that her memory may be so honored and ever cherished.

il-17031-bos-matter-81468.title:
PROPOSED RESOLUTION

COOK COUNTY RECOGNIZES OCTOBER 2026 AS DOMESTIC VIOLENCE AWARENESS MONTH (DVAM)

WHEREAS, Domestic Violence Awareness Month (DVAM) is observed nationally each October to raise awareness of domestic violence and its impact on individuals, families, and communities, with Congress formally recognizing the observance in 1989; and

WHEREAS, Domestic Violence Awareness Month provides an opportunity to uplift the voices, experiences, and resilience of survivors, educate the public about domestic violence, and strengthen support for individuals and families affected by abuse; and

WHEREAS, domestic violence is a pattern of physical, sexual, psychological, or emotional abuse, threats, intimidation, isolation, or economic coercion used by one person to establish and maintain power and control over another within a dating, familial, or household relationship; and

WHEREAS, intimate partner violence can occur at any stage of a relationship and affects individuals of all ages, racial and ethnic backgrounds, gender identities, sexual orientations, socioeconomic statuses, and religious affiliations; and

WHEREAS, according to the National Coalition Against Domestic Violence (NCADV), 1 in 4 women and 1 in 10 men experience sexual violence, physical violence, and/or stalking by an intimate partner during their lifetime; and

WHEREAS, women between the ages of 18 and 24 experience particularly high rates of intimate partner violence, underscoring the importance of early intervention, education, and prevention efforts; and

WHEREAS, access to a firearm in an abusive relationship substantially increases the risk of a fatal outcome, making effective firearm-removal protections an essential component of domestic violence prevention and survivor safety; and

WHEREAS, according to National Coalition Against Domestic Violence, 1 in 15 children in the United States is exposed to intimate partner violence each year, and approximately 90% of these children are eyewitnesses to the violence; and

WHEREAS, an estimated 15.5 million children in the United States live in families in which intimate partner violence has occurred at least once during the past year, highlighting the profound effects of domestic violence on children, families, and future generations; and

WHEREAS, survivors who are lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, or members of other sexual and gender minority communities may encounter additional barriers to accessing safety and support, including discrimination, stigma, and a lack of inclusive shelter and service options; and

WHEREAS, intimate partner violence affects people across sexual orientations, with 43.8% of lesbian women and 61.1% of bisexual women, compared with 35% of heterosexual women, reporting rape, physical violence, and/or stalking by an intimate partner; and

WHEREAS, men also experience intimate partner violence across sexual orientations, with 29% of heterosexual men, 26% of gay men, and 37.3% of bisexual men reporting rape, physical violence, and/or stalking by an intimate partner; and

WHEREAS, intimate partner violence affects women across racial and ethnic groups, with reported lifetime experiences of sexual violence, physical violence, and/or stalking by an intimate partner among 47% of American Indian and Alaska Native women, 45.1% of non-Hispanic Black women, 37.3% of non-Hispanic White women, 34.4% of Hispanic/Latina women, and 18.3% of Asian American and Pacific Islander women; and

WHEREAS, immigrant and noncitizen survivors may face additional barriers to seeking assistance, including concerns about immigration status, uncertainty surrounding changing immigration policies, and fear of law enforcement or immigration enforcement; and

WHEREAS, according to the Illinois Coalition Against Domestic Violence (ICADV), Illinois experienced a 26% decrease in domestic violence-related deaths in 2025 following a 140% increase in fatalities between 2022 and 2024; however, 72 domestic violence homicide incidents resulting in 101 total deaths in 2025--underscore the continued urgency of preventing domestic violence and protecting lives; and

WHEREAS, Karina’s Law took effect on May 11, 2025, strengthening firearm-removal protections under Illinois law for individuals subject to qualifying orders of protection and establishing additional procedures for the seizure of firearms and firearm parts when statutory requirements are met; named in honor of Karina Gonzalez and her daughter, Daniela Alvarez, who were killed in an act of domestic violence in Chicago in 2023, the law honors their lives by advancing efforts to protect survivors and prevent further loss of life; and

WHEREAS, the passage of Karina’s Law and the advocacy surrounding its enactment have elevated public awareness of domestic violence and strengthened efforts to improve survivor safety, reinforce accountability, and prevent domestic violence-related deaths; and

WHEREAS, in 2025, the Illinois Domestic Violence Hotline recorded a record-breaking 69,748 contacts through calls, text messages, and online chats, representing a 17% increase from 2024 and an 18% increase from 2019; and

WHEREAS, contacts to the Illinois Domestic Violence Hotline from the City of Chicago increased by 122% in 2025 compared with pre-pandemic levels in 2019, further demonstrating the growing demand for accessible and comprehensive domestic violence services; and

WHEREAS, domestic violence can have profound and lasting effects on the mental, emotional, and physical well-being of survivors, who may experience post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), anxiety, depression, suicidal thoughts, and substance use disorders; and

WHEREAS, research cited by the National Resource Center on Domestic Violence indicates that survivors who work with advocates experience less violence over time, report a higher quality of life and greater social support, and encounter fewer difficulties accessing community resources; and

WHEREAS, sustained investment in domestic violence prevention, crisis intervention, survivor advocacy, emergency shelter, counseling, legal assistance, and related support services is essential to protecting survivors, promoting healing, and preventing future violence throughout Cook County and across the nation; and
WHEREAS, Cook County residents who may be experiencing or witnessing domestic violence are encouraged to contact the Illinois Domestic Violence Hotline, available 24 hours a day, seven days a week, by calling or texting 877-863-6338 (877-TO END DV) for confidential support; and

WHEREAS, October is recognized nationally as Domestic Violence Awareness Month, and the third Thursday of October is observed as Purple Thursday, when individuals are encouraged to wear purple to demonstrate solidarity with survivors and raise awareness of domestic violence; and

WHEREAS, raising awareness, amplifying survivors’ voices, expanding access to essential services, and strengthening community-wide prevention efforts are critical to addressing domestic violence and building safer and healthier communities; and

NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the Cook County Board of Commissioners hereby commends domestic violence victim advocates, service providers, crisis hotline staff, first responders, and all individuals and organizations dedicated to preventing domestic violence and supporting survivors for their unwavering commitment, compassionate service, and tireless efforts to protect individuals and families; and

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the Cook County Board of Commissioners reaffirms its commitment to raising awareness of domestic violence and its devastating impact on individuals, families, and communities; promoting access to prevention, intervention, and survivor support services; and advancing collaborative efforts to address and eliminate domestic violence; and

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the Cook County Board of Commissioners hereby designates October 2026 as Domestic Violence Awareness Month in Cook County and encourages all Cook County residents, community organizations, businesses, and public agencies to speak out against domestic violence, stand in solidarity with survivors, support access to safety and healing, and work collectively toward a future free from domestic violence.

il-17031-bos-matter-81469.title:
PROPOSED RESOLUTION

COOK COUNTY RECOGNIZES OCTOBER 2026 AS BREAST CANCER AWARENESS MONTH
           
WHEREAS, October is nationally recognized as Breast Cancer Awareness Month, an annual campaign dedicated to increasing public awareness of breast cancer and emphasizing the importance of early detection, timely diagnosis, treatment, and access to care; and

WHEREAS, breast cancer is a significant global public health concern, affecting millions of individuals each year, and is a complex disease characterized by the uncontrolled growth of cells in breast tissue; and

WHEREAS, although breast cancer predominantly affects women, men can also develop the disease and face significant health risks; and

WHEREAS, according to the National Breast Cancer Foundation, approximately one in eight women and one in 726 men in the United States will be diagnosed with breast cancer during their lifetime; and

WHEREAS, according to the American Cancer Society, an estimated 321,910 women and 2,670 men in the United States will be diagnosed with invasive breast cancer in 2026, in addition to approximately 60,730 new cases of non-invasive (in situ) breast cancer; and

WHEREAS, breast cancer is the most diagnosed cancer among women in the United States, after skin cancer, and is the leading cause of cancer-related death among Hispanic/Latina women; and

WHEREAS, according to the National Breast Cancer Foundation, half of all women in the United States diagnosed with breast cancer are age 62 or younger, approximately 10% of new breast cancer cases occur in women younger than 45, and individuals diagnosed before age 35 face a greater risk of recurrence, underscoring the importance of breast cancer awareness, timely medical evaluation, continued monitoring, appropriate follow-up care, and research into the unique needs of younger patients; and

WHEREAS, an estimated 42,140 women in the United States are projected to die from breast cancer in 2026, and, on average, a woman in the United States is diagnosed with the disease approximately every two minutes; and

WHEREAS, despite these sobering statistics, more than four million breast cancer survivors are living in the United States, reflecting advances in research, treatment, and early detection; and

WHEREAS, according to the American Cancer Society, the breast cancer death rate among women in the United States declined by 44% from its peak in 1989 through 2022, resulting in nearly 518,000 fewer deaths than would have occurred had death rates remained unchanged; and

WHEREAS, approximately 66 % of breast cancer cases are diagnosed at a localized stage, before the cancer has spread beyond the breast, when treatment is generally more effective; and

WHEREAS, early detection through regular screenings, clinical examinations, and timely follow-up care can lead to better treatment outcomes and improved chances of survival, with more than 99% of individuals diagnosed with localized breast cancer surviving at least five years; and

WHEREAS, the American Cancer Society recommends that women at average risk of breast cancer have the option to begin annual mammography screening at age 40, with women ages 45 to 54 advised to receive annual mammograms and women age 55 and older able to transition to biennial screening or continue annual screening, underscoring the importance of informed screening decisions and access to preventive care; and

WHEREAS, approximately 40 million screening mammograms are performed annually in the United States, along with an estimated 1.7 million diagnostic mammograms, demonstrating the important role of breast imaging in detection and diagnosis; and

WHEREAS, breast cancer risk is influenced by several factors, including age and family history, and a woman's risk is nearly doubled if she has a first-degree relative, such as a mother, sister, or daughter, who has been diagnosed with the disease; and

WHEREAS, significant racial and ethnic disparities persist in breast cancer incidence, diagnosis, treatment, and outcomes, reflecting the need to address barriers to screening, timely diagnosis, and equitable access to quality care; and

WHEREAS, one in five Black women with breast cancer are diagnosed with triple-negative breast cancer-a subtype that is more aggressive and harder to treat-at a higher rate than any other racial or ethnic group; and 

WHEREAS, Hispanic/Latina women are more likely than White women to be diagnosed with breast cancer at later stages, when treatment may be more complex and outcomes less favorable; and

WHEREAS, according to data from the American Cancer Society, Asian American and Pacific Islander women are experiencing the fastest increases in breast cancer incidence, with annual increases of approximately 2.5% among women younger than 50 and 2.7% among women age 50 and older; and

WHEREAS, breast cancer awareness, education, research, equitable access to screening and treatment, and continued support for patients and survivors are essential to reducing disparities, improving outcomes, and saving lives; and

WHEREAS, during Breast Cancer Awareness Month, Cook County joins communities across the nation in honoring breast cancer survivors, remembering those who have lost their lives to the disease, supporting individuals currently undergoing treatment and their loved ones, and advocating for accessible health education, screening, and treatment resources;

NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the Cook County Board of Commissioners hereby recognizes and honors all individuals affected by breast cancer, including patients, survivors, caregivers, and their families; acknowledges their courage, strength, and resilience; and solemnly remembers those whose lives have been lost to the disease; and

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the Cook County Board of Commissioners hereby proclaims October 2026 as Breast Cancer Awareness Month in Cook County and reaffirms its commitment to promoting breast cancer awareness, advancing equitable access to screening and treatment, supporting patients and survivors, and encouraging continued education and research to improve outcomes for all individuals affected by breast cancer.

il-17031-bos-matter-81472.title:
PROPOSED RESOLUTION

RESOLUTION HONORING THE LIFE AND LEGACY OF CHEF SHONYA “CHEF ROYCE” WILLIAMS

WHEREAS, the Cook County Board of Commissioners recognizes the life and legacy of individuals whose contributions enrich their communities and leave a lasting impact on the lives of others; and

WHEREAS, Chef Shonya “Chef Royce” Williams, born January 16, 1971, in Chicago, Illinois, to Doris Williams and Eddie Wade, was a beloved mother, entrepreneur, culinary artist, and community builder whose life was defined by faith, resilience, creativity, and service; and

WHEREAS, a proud product of Chicago Public Schools, Chef Royce pursued her passion for culinary arts and transformed her talent into a successful entrepreneurial journey, launching Brown Bag Lady, opening Soule in Chicago’s Austin community, establishing Bugi’s in Berwyn and Danville, and later pursuing her passion for beauty through Kiss My Lashe Studio; and

WHEREAS, in May 2023, Chef Royce opened Soul Prime, celebrating her ancestors, heritage, and culture through elevated soul food and memorable dining experiences that brought families and communities together; and

WHEREAS, her culinary excellence earned her recognition, including a Presidential Lifetime Achievement Award in 2025, first place in a citywide chili competition in 2022, and acclaim from media outlets, food influencers, and culinary critics; and

WHEREAS, beyond her professional accomplishments, Chef Royce’s greatest joy was her family, particularly her beloved sons, Tot Williams, Kameron Williams, and Mekhi Williams, affectionately known as her “3-piece”; and

WHEREAS, Chef Royce transitioned from this life on October 4, 2026, leaving to cherish her memory her mother, Doris Williams; her sons; her siblings; her granddaughter; extended family; cherished friends; devoted staff; and countless members of the culinary community whose lives she touched; and

WHEREAS, Chef Royce’s legacy extends beyond the kitchen through the businesses she built, the traditions she honored, the opportunities she created, and the love she shared with her family and community; and

WHEREAS, the Cook County Board of Commissioners extends its heartfelt condolences to the Williams family and all who mourn her passing while celebrating a life that exemplified perseverance, Black entrepreneurship, and the enduring power of food to bring people together;

NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the President and Members of the Cook County Board of Commissioners do hereby honor the life and legacy of Chef Shonya “Chef Royce” Williams for her contributions to the culinary arts, Black entrepreneurship, and the communities of Chicago and beyond; and

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the Cook County Board of Commissioners extends its deepest sympathies to her family and loved ones and directs that a suitable copy of this resolution be presented to the family in recognition of her extraordinary life and enduring legacy.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that this resolution be spread upon the official record of proceedings of the Cook County Board of Commissioners.

il-17031-bos-matter-81473.title:
PROPOSED RESOLUTION

A RESOLUTION RECOGNIZING OCTOBER 2026 AS LGBTQ+ HISTORY MONTH IN COOK COUNTY 

WHEREAS, in July of 1961, Illinois became the first state to decriminalize homosexuality by repealing our sodomy laws; and  
 
WHEREAS, in 1952, homosexuality was classified as a mental disorder in the first edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM), and it wasn’t until 2013 that such categorizations of homosexuality as a mental illness were removed; and  
 
WHEREAS, on April 27, 1953, President Dwight D. Eisenhower signed an executive order that banned homosexuals from working for the federal government, sighting them as a security risk; and  
 
WHEREAS, on September 11, 1961, the first US-televised documentary about homosexuality aired on a local station in California; and  
 
WHEREAS, the Stonewall Riots occurred in New York City on June 28, 1969, led by Marsha P. Johnson, Silvia Rivera, Stormé DeLarverie, and Miss Major, and marked the beginning of the modern LGBTQIA+ rights movement, although previous demonstrations and organizing efforts amongst the LGBTQIA+ community preceded; and  
 
WHEREAS, on January 1, 1973, Maryland became the first state to statutorily ban same-sex marriage; and  
 
WHEREAS, in 1974, Kathy Kozachenko became the first openly LGBTQ American elected to any public office when she won a seat on the Ann Arbor, Michigan City Council; and  
 
WHEREAS, on October 14, 1979, the first National March on Washington for Lesbian and Gay Rights takes place, drawing an estimated 75,000 to 125,000 individuals marching for LGBTQ rights; and 
 
WHEREAS, on September 24, 1982, the CDC uses the term “AIDS” (Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome) for the first time in a new MMWR (Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report), and releases the first case definition for AIDS as “A disease at least moderately predictive of a defect in cell-mediated immunity, occurring in a person with no known cause for diminished resistance to that disease”; and  
 
WHEREAS, on October 11, 1988, the first National Coming Out Day was observed; and 
 
WHEREAS, the first World AIDS Day was observed on December 1, 1988; and  
 
WHEREAS, on November 30, 1993, President Bill Clinton signed the military policy known as “Don’t Ask, Don’t Tell,” a directive that prohibited openly gay and lesbian Americans from serving in the military; and  
 
WHEREAS, on September 21, 1996, President Clinton signed the Defense of Marriage Act, banning federal recognition of same-sex marriage and defining marriage as “a legal union between one man and one woman as husband and wife”; and  
 
WHEREAS, on December 3, 1996, Hawaii’s Judge Chang ruled that the state does not have a legal right to deprive same-sex couples of the right to marry, making Hawaii the first state to recognize that gay and lesbian couples are entitled to the same privileges as heterosexual married couples; and  
 
WHEREAS, on Jun 26, 2003, the Supreme Court decided Lawrence v. Texas, and held that a Texas statute criminalizing “homosexual conduct” violated the 14th Amendment’s Due Process Clause; and  
 
WHEREAS, on May 17, 2004, the first legal same-sex marriage in the United States took place in Massachusetts; and  
 
WHEREAS, on October 25, 2006, the New Jersey Supreme Court ruled that state lawmakers must provide the rights and benefits of marriage to gay and lesbian couples; and  
 
WHEREAS, on November 4, 2008, voters approve Proposition 8 in California, which made same-sex marriage illegal, and it wasn’t until 2010 that the proposition was found to be unconstitutional by a federal judge; and  
 
WHEREAS, on September 20, 2011, “Don’t Ask, Don’t Tell” is repealed, ending the ban on gay men and lesbians from serving openly in the military; and  
 
WHEREAS, on June 26, 2013, the Supreme Court held that Section 3 of the Defense of Marriage Act (DOMA), which denied federal recognition of same-sex marriages, was a violation of the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment; and  
 
WHEREAS, on November 20, 2013, same-sex marriage was passed in Illinois and signed into law by Governor Pat Quinn, with the law taking effect on June 1, 2014; and  
 
WHEREAS, on June 26, 2015, the Supreme Court ruled in Obergefell v. Hodges that states cannot ban same-sex marriage; and  
 
WHEREAS, on June 30, 2016, Secretary of Defense Carter announced that the Pentagon lifted the ban on transgender people serving openly in the US military; and  
 
WHEREAS, on March 23, 2018, the Trump administration announced a new policy that banned most transgender people from serving in the military, and the the Supreme Court allowed the ban to go into effect in January 2019; and  
 
WHEREAS, on June 15, 2020, the Supreme Court ruled in Bostock v. Clayton County that the 1964 Civil Rights Act protects gay, lesbian, and transgender employees from discrimination based on sex; and  
 
WHEREAS, on January 25, 2021, President Joe Biden signed an executive order repealing the 2019 ban on most transgender Americans joining the military; and  
 
WHEREAS, on December 13, 2022, President Biden signed the Respect for Marriage Act which included new federal protections for same-sex and interracial couples and officially voided the Defense of Marriage Act; and  
 
WHEREAS, many historic LGBTQ+ individuals have changed the world both within their community as well as in the wider geopolitical context; and 
 
WHEREAS, such individuals include Josephine Baker, a well-known entertainer of the Jazz Age who identified as bisexual, who was one of the most successful Black performers in French history and used her platform as an entertainer to advocate for desegregation, refusing to perform in segregated venues,  speaking at the 1963 March on Washington, and most notably serving as a spy for the French during World War II, passing along secrets she heard while performing for German soldiers; and  
 
WHEREAS, other notable individuals include Frida Kahlo, a gifted painter and openly bisexual artist who used her medium to depict taboo topics, like female sexuality, pain, and feminine beauty standards, primarily through self-portraits; and  
 
WHEREAS, the "father" of modern computer science, Alan Turing, was a key player in World War II serving as a cryptanalyst for the Allies and cracked the Nazi Enigma code - however, despite his service, Turing was prosecuted by his government for being in a homosexual relationship and was sentenced to chemical castration; and  
 
WHEREAS, Bayard Rustin was an openly gay Black man who was one of the major proponents of the nonviolent actions of Civil Rights protests and served as a close advisor to Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. And was one of the key organizers of the March on Washington; and 
 
WHEREAS, acclaimed American writer and civil rights activist, James Baldwin, garnered acclaim for his essays, novels, plays, and poems and pioneered depictions of men who loved other men, often across the lines of color and nationality, in works such as “Giovanni’s Room”, “Tell Me How Long the Train’s Been Gone”, “Another Country”, and “Just Above My Head”; and  
 
WHEREAS, many acclaimed writers and novelists belong to the LGBTQ+ community as well including Walt Whitman, Oscar Wilde, Emily Dickinson, and Virginia Woolf; and 
 
WHEREAS, even some of our most well-known historical individuals, such as Julius Caesar, Alexander the Great, Leonardo DaVinci, and Isaac Newton led lives that have strongly suggested to researchers and historians that they too belonged to the LGBTQ+ community; and  
 
WHEREAS, these events and people comprise just a small proportion of the extensive history pertaining to the LGBTQ+ community; and   
 
WHEREAS, these historically significant dates, events, and facts are not widely known nor taught; and  
 
WHEREAS, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender, and Queer (LGBTQ+) History Month is observed each year in the month of October to center and celebrate the history, successes, stories, work, and ongoing issues of the community; and   
 
WHEREAS, LGBTQ+ History Month was founded in 1994 by Rodney Wilson, a high school history teacher in Missouri, and passed as a resolution by the General Assembly of the National Education Association in 1995 which included LGBTQ+ History Month within a list of commemorative months; and  
 
WHEREAS, the month of October was selected to coincide with National Coming Out Day (Oct. 11), and the anniversary of the first march on Washington, and to correlate when schools are in session-providing a time and space for education on the history of the LGBTQ+ community; and  
 
WHEREAS, the LGBTQ+ community is an important contributor to the diverse and vibrant communities across Cook County, and are deserving of a time and space for us all to recognize and appreciate the role of LGBTQ+ people across World and American history; and  
 
WHEREAS, here in Cook County there has never been more LGBTQ+ representation by our elected officials; and 
 
WHEREAS, it remains essential that we continue to study and teach our neighbors and community members about the longstanding history of the LGBTQ+ community, their achievements, and impact on our world in the face of those who seek to eliminate them from our society; and  
 
WHEREAS, through the power of education, we as a County and a society can better understand the ways that past perspectives, laws, and treatment regarding the LGBTQ+ community continue to impact us today, and help us better advocate for LGBTQ+ members’ ongoing needs and rights;  
 
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the President and the Cook County Board of Commissioners, hereby proclaim the month of October 2026 to be LGBTQ+ History Month in Cook County.

il-17031-bos-matter-81474.title:
PROPOSED RESOLUTION

RECOGNIZING OCTOBER 11TH AS NATIONAL COMING OUT DAY 

WHEREAS, the first National Coming Out Day, organized by Jean O’Leary and Dr. Robert Eichberg with the National Coming Out Day organization, was observed on October 11, 1988, on the first anniversary of the National March on Washington for Lesbian and Gay Rights; and  
 
WHEREAS, National Coming Out Day is observed annually to celebrate and welcome those in the LGBTQ+ community who are ‘out’ or open about their identity and to raise awareness of the LGBTQ+ community and civil rights movement; and  
 
WHEREAS, the first National Coming Out Day had participation from eighteen states and garnered national media coverage, by its second year the holiday had participation from 21 states, and by 1990 National Coming Out Day was observed in all 50 states and several other countries; and  
 
WHEREAS, today, National Coming Out Day is observed internationally in countries including Ireland, Switzerland, the Netherlands, United Kingdom, and Portugal; and  
 
WHEREAS, studies have demonstrated the immense mental health benefits for members of the LGBTQ+ community who are ‘out’, including a 2013 study from the University of Montreal that found that lesbians, gay men, and bisexual people who were ‘out’ all had lower levels of biomarkers related to stress (such as cortisol, adrenaline, and blood pressure) than peers who were still in the closet; and  
 
WHEREAS, moreover, a 2018 study from the Journal of Adolescent Health found that when young transgender people used their chosen names, they reported fewer incidents of suicidal thoughts and behaviors, as well as less depressive symptoms; and  
 
WHEREAS, as we celebrate those who have made the brave decision to proudly announce their identity and have connection and support within the LGBTQ+ community, it remains important to acknowledge and embrace those who are still ‘in the closet’ or have chosen not to disclose their identity due to fears of violence, rejection, or hate crimes from their family, friends, peers, or co-workers; and  
 
WHEREAS, National Coming Out Day serves as a day to learn how to best support someone if and when they come out to you such as listening to them without judgement, letting them know you support and accept them no matter what, and asking them what they need from you; and  
 
WHEREAS, here in Cook County, we work every day to ensure our community is one of acceptance, support, and inclusion for all residents no matter their identity and whether they are out or not; and  
 
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the Cook County Board of Commissioners do hereby recognize October 11th as National Coming Out Day, and celebrates all those within the LGBTQ+ Community and their brave decision to be open about who they are.

il-17031-bos-matter-81476.title:
PROPOSED RESOLUTION

A RESOLUTION CONDEMNING THE DEATHLY IMPACT OF USAID CUTS ON GLOBAL HEALTH 

WHEREAS, in 1998, Congress established the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) as a functionally independent executive agency through the Foreign Affairs Reform and Restructuring Act; and  
 
WHEREAS, under this Act, President Bill Clinton reorganized USAID, which retained its independence from the U.S. Department of State, with its administrator reporting to and being under the direct authority and foreign policy guidance of the Secretary of State; and  
 
WHEREAS, U.S. citizens contribute about 17 cents per day to USAID, around just $64 per year; and  
 
WHEREAS, a study co-authored by a UCLA Fielding School of Public Health found that USAID-supported programs were associated with a 15% reduction in all-cause mortality and a 32% reduction in mortality among children under the age of 5 between 2001 and 2021; and  
 
WHEREAS, in countries receiving high levels of support, mortality from HIV/AIDS was reduced by 74%, malaria by 53%, and other tropical diseases by 51%; and  
 
WHEREAS, the study estimates that more than 91 million deaths were prevented between 2001 and 2021, of which approximately 30 million were children; and 
 
WHEREAS, under President George W. Bush, Congress passed the United States Leadership Against HIV/AIDS, Tuberculosis, and Malaria Act in 2003, creating the President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) to address the global HIV/AIDS epidemic and help save the lives of those suffering from the disease; and  
 
WHEREAS, PEPFAR is the largest commitment by any nation to address a single disease in history, enabled by strong bipartisan support across ten U.S. congresses and four presidential administrations; and  
 
WHEREAS, per its authorizing statute, PEPFAR is overseen by a U.S. Global AIDS Coordinator - a Senate-confirmed position appointed by the President and holding the rank of ambassador - at the State Department’s Bureau of Global Health Security and Diplomacy; and  
 
WHEREAS, USAID is PEPFAR’s largest government implementing agency, accounting for roughly 60% of PEPFAR’s bilateral assistance; and  
 
WHEREAS, PEPFAR works closely with partner countries toward achieving HIV/AIDS epidemic control while promoting the long-term sustainability of their responses; and  
 
WHEREAS, since PEPFAR’S inception, the U.S. government has invested over $100 billion in the global HIV/AIDS response, saved 26 million lives, and enabled 7.8 million babies to be born without HIV infection; and   
 
WHEREAS, Studies have also found that PEPFAR funding has been associated with several “spillover” effects including significant reductions in all-cause mortality, increases in childhood immunizations, and increases in GDP growth; and  
 
WHEREAS, PEPFAR has been reauthorized by Congress four times, most recently in March 2024 for just one year; and 
 
WHEREAS, PEPFAR’s authorization was not renewed and expired on March 25, 2025; and 
 
WHEREAS, on March 10, 2025, The Trump administration announced they had officially cancelled 86% of U.S. foreign aid contracts; and  
 
WHEREAS, studies have crucially found that the recent cuts to USAID may lead to more than 14 million additional deaths globally by 2030, including more than 4.5 million children under 5; and 
WHEREAS, an analysis found that of the 770 global health awards identified, 379 included HIV activities, 71% of which were terminated, including several HIV treatment awards as well as most HIV prevention; and  
 
WHEREAS, former civil servant at USAID Nicholas Enrich projected that with these cuts, and assuming they are not restored, an additional one million children will die every year; and  
 
WHEREAS, Enrich also projected that up to 17.9 million more people will contract malaria and as many as 166,000 people will die from it constituting a 39% increase from current rates; and  
 
WHEREAS, additional projections suggest that Tuberculosis cases, including multidrug-resistant TB, will soar by 28 to 32 percent; and  
 
WHEREAS, with these cuts, as many as 28,000 people will suffer from emerging infectious diseases, like Ebola and Marburg; and  
 
WHEREAS, hundreds of millions of people will contract polio infections over the next decade, with an additional 200,000 people becoming paralyzed by polio; and  
 
WHEREAS, Enrich also noted that the cuts could lead to "increasing the likelihood of unchecked outbreaks of emerging infectious diseases such as avian influenza, Ebola, and mpox - threats that can spread globally and endanger American citizens; and  
 
WHEREAS, the sudden withdrawal of U.S. money has caused a systemic shock, with U.N. officials warning that, if the funding isn’t replaced, the cuts could lead to more than 4 million AIDS-related deaths and 6 million more HIV infections by 2029; and  
 
WHEREAS, as a result of these cuts to PEPFAR and USAID, as of July 2026, so far 1,700 global sites providing preventative medicine and treatment have been closed; and  
 
WHEREAS, as of this year, 73 percent of groups that provide services to particularly vulnerable groups, sex workers, men who have sex with men, people who use injection drugs, reported that they have stopped providing at least one type of service; and  
 
WHEREAS, recent reports from 22 neonatal clinics in a network of hospitals in Africa where newborns come to, found that mothers had a 50 percent jump in HIV rates and over 300 percent jump in those places finding women were not on treatment; and  
 
WHEREAS, following these cuts, a tracking survey found that PrEP initiations declined by 13 percent and 66 percent in five high-burden countries between January-September 2024 and January-September 2025 
 
WHEREAS, a recent analysis in 14 countries found that the disruption in PEPFAR funding was associated with significant drops in access from early 2025 through early 2026 and that recovery remains limited, with ongoing reduced access to HIV services and commodities, including antiretroviral treatment, PrEP, HIV tests, and clinical monitoring tests; and  
 
WHEREAS, the ramifications of these cuts to PEPFAR and USAID inevitably trickle down into the lives, communities, and medical systems of residents within Cook County; and  
 
WHEREAS, Cook County continues to advocate for health equity, promoting education and awareness, and supporting organizations that work tirelessly to serve those at risk and living with HIV and AIDS;  
 
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the Cook County Board of Commissioners does hereby issue its full condemnation of the Trump Administrations’ cuts to USAID and PEPFAR funding, demand the immediate reinstatement of this funding, and mourn the deaths that have and will occur if these cuts are not reversed.

il-17031-bos-matter-81478.title:
PROPOSED ORDINANCE AMENDMENT

REQUIRING SEMI-ANNUAL REPORTING ON USE OF AUTOMATIC LICENSE PLATE READERS BY COOK COUNTY SHERIFF’S OFFICE  

BE IT ORDAINED, by the Cook County Board of Commissioners, that Chapter 46, Article II, Division 1, Sec. 46-37.1 of the Cook County Code is hereby amended as Follows: 

Sec. 46-37.1. - Quarterly reporting.

(a)	The Sheriff's Office shall report to the Board of Commissioners quarterly on the cost that the office incurs due to investigating and processing cases involving firearms.
 
(b)	The Sheriff’s Office shall submit and present to the Board of Commissioners a semi-annual report concerning the use, oversight, and safeguards associated with its Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) technology. Such reporting shall focus on documented investigative use, compliance with established policies, auditing procedures, data privacy protections, and measures taken to prevent and address unauthorized use.  The semi-annual reports shall include the following:

(1)	Investigative Use and Accountability 

Information concerning the use of ALPR technology for authorized law enforcement purposes, including:

a.	The number of investigative queries conducted.  
b.	The number of investigations in which ALPR information was documented as having been utilized.   
c.	 Compliance with requirements for documenting a legitimate law enforcement purpose, criminal investigative predicate, and associated case or incident number.

(2)	Auditing and Policy Compliance

Information concerning the Sheriff’s Office’s oversight and auditing of ALPR use, including: 

a.	The number of audits conducted and investigative queries reviewed. 
b.	The scope and methodology of audits conducted during the reporting period. 
c.	The number of potential policy violations identified through auditing or other oversight mechanisms
d.	Aggregate statistical information regarding the disposition of substantiated violations and any resulting corrective actions, including retraining, suspension, or revocation of system access, or disciplinary referrals, as applicable. 

(3)	Data Privacy and Access Safeguards

Information concerning the security of ALPR information, including:

a.	Compliance with established data retention and deletion requirements.  
b.	Enforcement of authorized user access restrictions and authentication requirements. 
c.	Compliance with restrictions governing access to and sharing of ALPR information with all agencies that have executed a Declaration of Investigative Intentions for Access to Cook County Sheriff’s Office ALPR System (“ALPR Declaration”). 
d.	The number of identified incidents involving unauthorized access, use, or disclosure of ALPR information, if any, and the actions taken in response. 

(4)	Security and Data Protection

Information concerning the security of ALPR information, including:

a.	Any known identified security incidents or confirmed data breaches involving ALPR information. 
b.	Any substantiated violations of established data-sharing agreements or access restrictions involving all agencies that have executed an ALPR Declaration. 
c.	Actions taken to address identified vulnerabilities, prevent unauthorized access, and strengthen data security protections. 

Limitation of Disclosure of Security and Data Protection Measures. Disclosure under this Section 4 shall not include information about CCSO’s security system, access controls, or security vulnerabilities, including information relating to any third-party vendor’s software procured by the CCSO, the release of which could reasonably compromise CCSO’s network security, or the network security of a third-party vendor’s software, or reveal a third-party vendor’s proprietary information otherwise prohibited from disclosure. This Section does not limit disclosures required by CCSO under applicable law. 

(5)	Safeguards Implementation and Improvements

A summary of any material changes to ALPR policies, procedures, training requirements, access controls, or auditing protocols implemented during the reporting period to strengthen accountability, protect personal information, and ensure compliance with applicable requirements.

a.	Reports shall present information and data in aggregate form and shall not require the disclosure of personally identifiable information; confidential investigative information; information that would compromise an active investigation; information that would compromise or interfere with an internal disciplinary process; information that could reasonably compromise network security of CCSO, Cook County, a third-party vendor, or other law enforcement agency; information that could reasonably lead to the disclosure of a third-party vendor’s proprietary information that is otherwise prohibited from disclosure under law or by an agreement between relevant Parties; information relating to another law enforcement agency’s use of its own ALPR system that CCSO is not authorized to release; or information that is otherwise prohibited from disclosure pursuant to State or federal law.  
b.	Reporting shall emphasize documented investigative use, adherence to established safeguards, audit findings, and corrective actions. The total number of license plates passively captured by ALPR cameras shall not be required as a quarterly reporting metric, as such information does not independently establish how ALPR information is accessed, utilized, or managed by authorized personnel. 

Effective date:  This ordinance shall be in effect starting March 1, 2027.

il-17031-bos-matter-81481.title:
PROPOSED RESOLUTION

DECLARING OCTOBER 18 - 24, 2026 UNITED AGAINST HATE WEEK 

WHEREAS, United Against Hate Week is a nationwide call for local action to reject hate of any kind, and a resolve to build a safe and more equitable world together; and  

WHEREAS, Cook County United Against Hate launched in 2022 to activate individuals and communities to champion justice, report discrimination, and disrupt bullying and injustice everywhere it exists; and  

WHEREAS, Cook County United Against Hate is growing a diverse coalition of comprised of individuals as well as nearly 100 nonprofits, faith groups, businesses, academic organizations, and governments that publicly denounce bigotry; and 

WHEREAS, Cook County United Against Hate challenges everyone to foster welcoming communities, free from discrimination; and  

WHEREAS, Cook County United Against Hate creates opportunities to educate about the impacts of intolerance on ourselves, our neighbors, and our communities; and 

WHEREAS, the Cook County Sheriff’s Office, Forest Preserves Police, Public Defender, State’s Attorney, and Department of Human Rights support people and communities that are victims or witnesses of hate; and 

WHEREAS, Cook County is a sanctuary County that welcomes all people regardless of their race, religion, ethnicity, age, gender identity, sexual orientation, ability, class, or other backgrounds; and 

WHEREAS, hate crimes continue to rise and have more than doubled since 2015; and 

WHEREAS, nationally, according to the US Department of Justice, 10,881 hate crime incidents were reported in 2025; and 

WHEREAS, 10,528 single-bias incidents involved 12,967 offenses; and 

WHEREAS, despite a decline in reported hate crimes as compared to 2024, Black and Brown communities continue to bear the brunt of racially motivated hate and white supremacy; and   

WHEREAS, the figures in the FBI’s Crime Data Explorer reflect only the tip of the iceberg, as hate crimes are grievously underreported; and 

WHEREAS, of the 9,596 known hate crime offenders nationally, 56% were White, 20% were Black or African American, and 15% race unknown; and 

WHEREAS, in Illinois in 2025, 377 hate incidents were reported, with 56% of incidents against a person because of their race or ethnicity; and 

WHEREAS, according to the National Bullying Center for Education Statistics, one out of five students report being bullied; and 

WHEREAS, the cycle of violence escalates with each escaped consequence, and hateful rhetoric is radicalized to murderous ends; and  
WHEREAS, Cook County is steadfast in its commitment to fostering inclusion, where every resident, no matter their background or zip code, can live without fear of discrimination, harassment, or violence; and  

WHEREAS, creating belonging, inclusive, and welcoming spaces is hard and continuous work; and 

NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED, the Cook County Board of Commissioners does hereby declare October 18 - 24, 2026 as United Against Hate Week and recommits to welcoming all people regardless of their race, religion, ethnicity, age, gender identity, sexual orientation, ability, class, or other background; and 

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, the Cook County Board of Commissioners are committed to the Cook County United Against Hate Pledge, which asks us to actively learn from those with different lived experiences, question hateful acts, educate on how to safely interrupt and report hate, and support efforts towards justice; and 

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, during United Against Hate Week, and every week, Cook County encourages residents, governments, and organizations in every community to seek restorative justice to repair the damage of hate, discrimination, bullying, systemic racism, and violence; and 

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, hate against one is hate against all, and hate has no home in Cook County...end
